title: Sectors and economic structure

blocks.heading: Sectors and economic structure
blocks.text: Primary production obtains natural resources, secondary production processes materials into goods, and tertiary production supplies services. Sector employment shares show the distribution of employed people, not directly their productivity or well-being. Many development histories involve a declining share of agricultural employment and growth of industrial and service work, but countries vary. A falling agricultural share can occur while the number of agricultural workers increases if total employment grows faster. A service-sector job is not automatically well-paid. Interpret the supplied counts and definitions rather than applying a country stereotype.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Primary production
blocks.text: Primary production obtains products directly from natural resources, such as farming, fishing or mining. The primary-sector employment share is primary employment divided by total employment, multiplied by 100. Growing grain is primary activity; milling the grain is secondary activity. Use employed people as the denominator when the question asks for an employment share. The whole population includes people who are not employed and answers a different question.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Secondary production
blocks.text: Secondary production processes or manufactures materials into goods, including manufacturing and construction. The secondary-sector employment share is secondary employment divided by total employment, multiplied by 100. Turning timber into furniture illustrates secondary production. Transporting the furniture is a service. One product can therefore connect several sectors at different stages, while each activity is classified by what it does rather than the name of the final item.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Tertiary production
blocks.text: Tertiary production provides services, such as transport, teaching, retailing or repair. The tertiary-sector employment share is tertiary employment divided by total employment, multiplied by 100. Selling farm produce is tertiary activity even though growing it is primary. A service creates a useful activity rather than a new tangible object. The word tertiary does not mean optional or unproductive; a missing delivery service can prevent goods reaching users.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Calculate and interpret shares
blocks.text: In a synthetic district with 2,000 employed people, primary employment is 800, secondary 500 and tertiary 700. Primary share = 800 ÷ 2,000 = 0.4; multiplying by 100 gives 40%; secondary is 25% and tertiary 35%. Counts sum to 2,000 and shares to 100%. In another fictional district, shares are 20%, 30% and 50%. The second has a smaller primary share and larger service share, but the shares alone do not establish wages or job security. For separate practice, 450 of 1,500 is 30%, 360 of 1,200 is 30%, and 560 of 1,400 is 40%. Keep the sector count and denominator from the same dataset.
